implementation_notes: JavaScript has no checked failure channel, so the idiomatic replacement for the classic notification class is a plain result object: accumulate entries in an array and return { ok: errors.length === 0, value, errors }. The entries stay data (field, code, message) and go straight into a JSON response. AggregateError is the language's native multi-error container, but it is thrown and carries only Error instances, so it suits Promise.any-style fan-in rather than boundary validation; prefer the schema variant when the rules are declarative.
pitfalls: Nothing forces the caller to look at ok, so a forgotten check is silent; keep one result shape across the codebase so the check is idiomatic.
Mutating the input while validating couples diagnostics to side effects - validate a copy or leave the input untouched.
Throwing AggregateError to signal validation failures turns an expected outcome into an exception and loses the structured field paths.

variants.name: Zod schema safeParse
variants.implementation_notes: Schema-first validation packages the checks as data: z.object({...}).safeParse(input) returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error } where error.issues is the full list of problems (path, code, message) - parse() is the throwing variant to avoid at a boundary. Zod works in plain JavaScript as well as TypeScript; choose it when the same schema should also drive types, docs or OpenAPI.
pitfalls: parse() throws a ZodError; only safeParse() hands the errors back as a value, so mixing the two at a boundary reintroduces fail-fast.
A field stops at its first failing check while every field is still reported; dependent refinements must not assume earlier fields parsed.
issue.path is an array (including numeric indices inside collections); flattening it to a string loses where the failure sits.
